feedback.nudge: Six terms. For each $n$ from 1 to 6, $\P(X \ge n) = 1 - \bigl(\tfrac{n-1}{6}\bigr)^2$ because $X < n$ needs both rolls below $n$. Add them.

explanation:
## The six terms

$X \le n-1$ means both rolls are at most $n-1$, which by independence has probability $\bigl(\tfrac{n-1}{6}\bigr)^2$. So for $1 \le n \le 6$,

$$\P(X \ge n) = 1 - \frac{(n-1)^2}{36},$$

and $\P(X \ge n) = 0$ for $n \ge 7$.

| $n$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\P(X\ge n)$ | $\tfrac{36}{36}$ | $\tfrac{35}{36}$ | $\tfrac{32}{36}$ | $\tfrac{27}{36}$ | $\tfrac{20}{36}$ | $\tfrac{11}{36}$ |

$$\E X = \frac{36+35+32+27+20+11}{36} = \frac{161}{36} = 4.4\overline{7} .$$

Equivalently $\E X = 6 - \dfrac{0+1+4+9+16+25}{36} = 6 - \dfrac{55}{36}$.

## Why the formula is true

Write $X = \sum_{n \ge 1} I_{\{X \ge n\}}$ — for a non-negative integer $X$ exactly $X$ of those indicators are 1. Taking expectations and exchanging the sum with the expectation,

$$\E X = \sum_{n \ge 1} \E\,I_{\{X \ge n\}} = \sum_{n \ge 1} \P(X \ge n).$$

The exchange is legitimate because every term is non-negative (Theorem 1.8 in the notes), and that non-negativity is the only hypothesis. No independence, no finiteness assumed in advance: if the right side is infinite then so is $\E X$.

## When to reach for it

The direct route is $\E X = \sum_{k=1}^{6} k\,\P(X = k)$, which needs the probability mass function $\P(X=k) = \tfrac{2k-1}{36}$ — a small extra computation, because you have to difference the distribution function.

The tail formula skips that step. It is the better tool whenever $\P(X \ge n)$ is easier than $\P(X = n)$, and "the maximum of several things" is the standard case: $X \ge n$ fails only when *everything* is below $n$, which is a product, while $X = n$ needs an inclusion–exclusion.

The same shape appears throughout the course. The geometric distribution has $\P(X \ge n) = (1-p)^{n-1}$, so $\E X = \sum (1-p)^{n-1} = 1/p$ with no series manipulation at all — and Wald's identity, at the end of chapter 2, is proved with the same exchange of a sum and an expectation.
